questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical governance using ResourceQuota and LimitRange, including defaults, enforcement, and validation in real clusters.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped ResourceQuota hard limits
- LimitRange defaults for containers
- kubectl-based verification and testing
- Isolation in multi-tenant clusters

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: qa-tenant
spec:
hard:
  pods: "20"
  requests.cpu: "4"
  requests.memory: "4Gi"
  limits.cpu: "4"
  limits.memory: "4Gi"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: qa-tenant-defaults
spec:
limits:
- type: Container
  defaultRequest:
    cpu: "100m"
    memory: "128Mi"
  default:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: "256Mi"
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you audit namespace quotas over time?
- What happens if a pod requests more than the defaults?

## Why This Is Asked
Covers a common beginner pitfall: RBAC can block simple ConfigMap reads, breaking startup behavior. It tests practical debugging with kubectl and small RBAC fixes rather than theory.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes RBAC and ServiceAccounts
- ConfigMaps and their namespace scoping

## Code Example
```yaml
# Role granting read access to ConfigMaps in a namespace
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: configmap-reader
  namespace: my-namespace
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get"]
---
# Bind Role to the API Pod's ServiceAccount
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: api-sa-configmap-reader
  namespace: my-namespace
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: api-sa
  namespace: my-namespace
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: configmap-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

- How would you verify that the ConfigMap was actually mounted into the Pod?
- What could cause intermittent Forbidden errors even after the fix?

## Why This Is Asked

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper, ConstraintTemplate, Constraint, violations
- Rego rules for Pod security, matching exclusions

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (illustrative)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8spodsecurity
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sPodSecurityPolicy
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8spodsecurity
      violation[violation] {
        input.review.object.kind == "Pod"
        some container
        not input.review.object.spec.containers[_].securityContext.runAsNonRoot
      }
```

```yaml
# Constraint (illustrative)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sPodSecurityPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-ps
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    excludedNamespaces: ["kube-system"]
  parameters: {}
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests understanding of how NetworkPolicy impacts outbound traffic—a common production pitfall that can cause cascading service failures when egress restrictions are applied without proper allowlisting.

## Key Concepts
- **NetworkPolicy**: A namespace-scoped Kubernetes resource that controls traffic flow into and out of pods using pod selectors
- **Egress rules**: Define allowed outbound destinations using cidrBlocks, namespace selectors, and port specifications
- **Debugging workflow**: Inspect existing policies, test connectivity from within the cluster, and apply targeted policy exceptions

## Code Example
```bash
# List all NetworkPolicies in the cluster
kubectl get netpol -A

# Inspect egress rules for a specific NetworkPolicy
kubectl describe netpol <policy-name> -n <namespace>

# Deploy a debug pod for testing
e kubectl run debug-pod --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- /bin/sh

# Test connectivity to billing service from debug pod
kubectl exec -it debug-pod -- wget --spider <billing-service-url>:<port>

# Apply minimal egress NetworkPolicy to allow billing service traffic
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-billing-egress
  namespace: <api-namespace>
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  egress:
  - to:
    - pod: {}
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
EOF
```

Advanced Kubernetes engineers translate theory into concrete, scalable designs with real-world DR and upgrade considerations.

## Key Concepts
- StatefulSet, PVCs, and StorageClass
- Anti-affinity and PodDisruptionBudget
- Readiness/Liveness probes and rolling updates
- Etcd backup/DR and cross-AZ failover testing

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  serviceName: "example"
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: example
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: example
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-reg/app:latest
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you verify DR readiness after deployment?
- What changes to cluster autoscaler or etcd backup cadence would you consider for larger clusters?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of CRD versioning, conversion webhooks, and safe migrations in production-like settings.

- CRD versioning and conversion webhook lifecycle
- Backwards compatibility and migration planning
- Controller resilience during schema changes

apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: myapps.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema: { }
    subresources:
      status: {}
  conversion:
    strategy: Webhook
    webhook:
      clientConfig:
        service:
          name: myapp-conversion
          namespace: default
        caBundle: "<base64-ca>"
      conversionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
```

# SecretProviderClass example (Vault)
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: vault-creds
spec:
  provider: vault
  parameters:
    roleName: "db-role"
    vaultAddress: "https://vault.example.com"
    objects: |
      - objectName: db-credentials
        secretPath: secret/data/db/creds
        secretKey: creds
    refreshInterval: "3600s"
```

kubectl patch pvc db-2 -n default -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"150Gi"}}}}'

# Rolling restart (FS resize depends on driver; may auto-resize)
